## Instructions

# Instructions

Implement variable length quantity encoding and decoding.

The goal of this exercise is to implement [VLQ][vlq] encoding/decoding.

In short, the goal of this encoding is to encode integer values in a way that would save bytes.
Only the first 7 bits of each byte are significant (right-justified; sort of like an ASCII byte).
So, if you have a 32-bit value, you have to unpack it into a series of 7-bit bytes.
Of course, you will have a variable number of bytes depending upon your integer.
To indicate which is the last byte of the series, you leave bit #7 clear.
In all of the preceding bytes, you set bit #7.

So, if an integer is between `0-127`, it can be represented as one byte.
Although VLQ can deal with numbers of arbitrary sizes, for this exercise we will restrict ourselves to only numbers that fit in a 32-bit unsigned integer.
Here are examples of integers as 32-bit values, and the variable length quantities that they translate to:

```text
 NUMBER        VARIABLE QUANTITY
00000000              00
00000040              40
0000007F              7F
00000080             81 00
00002000             C0 00
00003FFF             FF 7F
00004000           81 80 00
00100000           C0 80 00
001FFFFF           FF FF 7F
00200000          81 80 80 00
08000000          C0 80 80 00
0FFFFFFF          FF FF FF 7F
```

[vlq]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable-length_quantity

def encode(numbers):
    encoded_bytes = []
    for n in numbers:
        if n == 0:
            encoded_bytes.append(0)
            continue

        # Temporary list to store 7-bit chunks in LSB-first order
        temp_7bit_chunks = []
        current_num = n 
        while current_num > 0:
            temp_7bit_chunks.append(current_num & 0x7F)
            current_num >>= 7

        # Construct VLQ bytes.
        # Iterate from the most significant 7-bit chunk to the least significant.
        # The least significant 7-bit chunk (which is temp_7bit_chunks[0])
        # will be the *last* byte in the VLQ sequence, so its MSB (continuation bit) will be 0.
        # All other chunks will be preceding bytes, so their MSB will be 1.
        for i in range(len(temp_7bit_chunks) - 1, -1, -1):
            byte = temp_7bit_chunks[i]
            if i > 0:  # If this is not the LSB 7-bit chunk, it's a preceding byte in the final VLQ sequence
                byte |= 0x80  # Set the continuation bit
            encoded_bytes.append(byte)

    return encoded_bytes


def decode(bytes_):
    decoded_numbers = []
    current_number = 0
    byte_index = 0
    
    # Define the maximum 32-bit unsigned integer value (0xFFFFFFFF)
    MAX_32_BIT_UNSIGNED = (1 << 32) - 1

    while byte_index < len(bytes_):
        byte = bytes_[byte_index]
        byte_index += 1

        seven_bits = byte & 0x7F  # Extract the lower 7 bits

        # Calculate the potential new current_number by shifting the existing bits left by 7
        # and adding the new 7 bits. Python's integers handle arbitrary size, so this
        # operation will not overflow within Python itself.
        test_number = (current_number << 7) | seven_bits

        # Check if the calculated number exceeds the 32-bit unsigned integer limit
        if test_number > MAX_32_BIT_UNSIGNED:
            raise ValueError("number exceeds 32-bit unsigned integer limit")
        
        current_number = test_number

        # Check the most significant bit (MSB, 0x80) to see if this is the last byte of a number
        if (byte & 0x80) == 0:  # MSB is 0, indicating this is the last byte for the current number
            decoded_numbers.append(current_number)
            current_number = 0  # Reset for the next number

    # After iterating through all bytes, if current_number is not 0, it means
    # a number was being built but was not terminated by a byte with MSB 0.
    if current_number != 0:
        raise ValueError("incomplete sequence")

    return decoded_numbers
